item.title: DQC Seminar Series: Quantum oblique eigenprojection — Thu Oct 22, 12:00 PM — None
item.description: Every square matrix decomposes its underlying Hilbert space into generalized, nonorthogonal eigensubspaces. We show that a quantum computer can perform such an oblique eigenprojection $\Pi$ given block encoding access to the input matrix. Our approach has a query complexity nearly linear in the inverse gap and a normalization factor close to $\lVert\Pi\rVert$ under a spectral-set condition on the input. This covers common assumptions on the numerical range or diagonalizability and matches known results for orthogonal eigenprojections. We achieve this with a two-sided block preconditioning that uses a discrete Fourier transform of the matrix resolvent. We describe applications to: (i) preparing eigenstates of matrices with complex eigenvalues, extending the quantum eigenvalue transformation algorithm of Low and Su beyond real spectra; (ii) solving continuous-time algebraic Riccati equations, cubically speeding up a prior solver of Rodenas-Ruiz, Zhao, and Lee; and (iii) solving ordinary

item.title: Mortality and Measurement: Race-Medicine, Statistics, and Empire — Thu Oct 22, 4:00 PM — Classroom Building
item.description:
Suman Seth is the Stephen H. Weiss Presidential Fellow and Marie Underhill Noll Professor of the History of Science at Cornell University.
This talk will offer an overview of Seth's forthcoming book from Cambridge University Press (2027), which seeks to make four interlocking arguments: First, that it was in medicine, rather than science, that we see the 'main game' for the development of naturalistic understandings of race in the nineteenth century; second, that a key locus for this development was to be found in medical statistics: the roots for much of our thinking about scientific uses of race today lie in the racialized statistics of the era of high imperialism; third, that the history of race must be written in an imperial and not merely a national register, a point that also requires us to see the history of slavery and its abolition as having effects well beyond the areas of its immediate application; and fourth, that the medicine of empire 'struck back' after the end of the N

item.title: What Does Cash Do For Children? Families, Income & Child Development in the US. — Thu Oct 22, 4:00 PM — Sanford School -- Rubenstein Hall
item.description: Katherine Magnuson Ph.D., Human Development and Social Policy, Northwestern University, 2002; B.A., History and Political Science, Brown University, 1995 Katherine's research focuses on the well-being and development of economically disadvantaged children and their families. She examines how disparities in socioeconomic status (SES) affect children's development, and how these effects may be altered by policies and programs, especially early childhood education programs. She also investigates how maternal education impacts child development. Specifically, Katherine blends two streams of research that are often considered separately: (1) research on the influence of parents' employment, income, and education, as well as welfare policies, on children's well-being, with a special emphasis on the extent to which differences in SES across racial and ethnic groups explain disparities in children's school performance; and (2) research on direct child interventions, particularly early educatio

item.description:
You are invited to a book talk with Duke alum Dr. Felicia Arriaga, AB'12, AM '15, PhD'18. Currently a professor at Baruch College, CUNY, Dr. Arriaga will discuss her 2023 book, "Behind Crimmigration" (UNC Press, 2023).
The book discussion will focus on the racial, economic, and political issues that have shaped federal, state, and local policies-including policies specific to North Carolina-that have led to increased enforcement in immigrant communities.
Born and raised in North Carolina, Dr. Arriaga earned her Bachelors, Masters and PhD at Duke University in Sociology while participating in student activism and local organizations. Dr. Arriaga is a public sociologist who has focused much on her work in collaborating with immigrant communities and exploring the impacts of immigration laws and related policies. She also serves as the Board Chair of the NC-based community organization, El Pueblo.

item.title: Mongane Wally Serote, Poet Laureate of South Africa — Thu Oct 22, 5:30 PM — East Duke 201 - Nelson Music Room
item.description:
Mongane Wally Serote, the Poet Laureate of South Africa will present an evening of poetry and reflections on the 50th anniversary of the Soweto Uprising, when students bravely fought back against apartheid education policies, and were met with shocking police violence. Serote is the author of numerous collections of poetry as well as 5 novels. Like the U.S. Black Arts Movement writers he befriended during years in exile, his work has taken inspiration from jazz, coming of age stories, and liberation traditions. He was a long-time anti-apartheid activist, and continues to advocate for a more just society through his literary and public activities. Duke is proud to welcome him for this presentation, which will be followed by conversation with the audience facilitated by Professor Tsitsi Jaji.
Source: Duke Arts, Duke University

item.title: “Cosmic Origins” Opening Reception — Thu Oct 22, 5:30 PM — Center for Documentary Studies
item.description:
Join us for the opening reception of "Cosmic Origins," a new exhibition by photographer and Duke MFA|EDA alumna Cassandra Klos.
Bringing together photographs, artifacts, and ephemera, "Cosmic Origins" explores humanity's relationship to space, scientific exploration, and the possibility of life beyond Earth. The exhibition features work from Klos's long-term project "Mars on Earth," which documents her experiences as an analog astronaut participating in Earth-based simulations designed to replicate the conditions, challenges, and isolation of future space missions.
Meet the artist, explore the exhibition, and enjoy light refreshments.
Organized by CDS in collaboration with Duke University's MFA|EDA program and the Duke SPACE Initiative, with support from Duke's Office of Interdisciplinary Programs. More info about the exhibition: https://documentarystudies.duke.edu/upcoming-exhibitions.
*Directions and Parking*

item.title: Carolina Performing Arts: Violinist Alexi Kenney and Pianist Janice Carissa — Thu Oct 22, 7:00 PM — Hill Hall
item.description:
Violinist Alexi Kenney and pianist Janice Carissa invite audiences to hear familiar works with fresh ears.
At the center of the program is The Wild Yes by composer and violinist Michi Wiancko, surrounded by music that spans geography, time, and tradition. The musical voices of composers Sibelius, Piazzolla, and inti figgis-vizueta enter the conversation, creating surprising relationships between sounds that might otherwise seem worlds apart.
Kenney and Carissa guide audiences through this remarkable musical landscape and remind us that great music is never fixed in time. Rather, it is continually revitalized by new listeners and fresh perspectives.
Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/alexi-kenney-janice-carissa/
Source: UNC Chapel Hill

item.title: Film Screening: “Zhuang Wei’s Witness: Return of the Survivor” (Zhuang Wei, 2026) — Thu Oct 22, 7:00 PM — Rubenstein Arts Center
item.description:
---Zhuang Wei, 2026, 89 min, China, Chinese with English subtitles---
Synopsis Returning to the unfamiliar Chaoshan homeland to live, I encountered my grand-uncle Ajun, who had returned from Cambodia.
Carrying stories of surviving the Khmer Rouge, he stirred my life as I tried to become a witness.
About the filmmaker: Zhuang Wei (A Zui, means "mouth" in Chinese), born in 1999, is a documentary filmmaker and freelance artist from Chaoshan, Guangdong. She also engages in artistic practices across different mediums that intervene in society.
In 2021, she joined the "Folk Memory Project" at Caochangdi Workstation, where she created the feature-length documentaries Zhuang Wei's Mouth (2024) and Zhuang Wei's Testimony: The Survivor Returns (2026). She is now processing her long-term filming in the ancestral village "Wushi Village."
Source: Duke Arts, Duke University

Frontier multimodal models handle familiar concepts well and struggle on niche ones: sorting drill-core samples into 35 geological classes, or telling adhesion from scarring on a ceramic substrate. item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Jan 19 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.description:
This talk is based on my recently published book, Wanting Children: Family-Planning Policies and the Engineering of America's Population (University of Chicago Press). Unlike most of the world, U.S. family-planning policy has focused almost exclusively on limiting fertility, with little attention to supporting people who want to have children. I trace the historical and political roots of this asymmetry and argue for a more balanced approach to population policy - one that takes seriously the needs of those who want to become parents. Drawing on population research, I'll discuss what a more supportive fertility policy should look like and why it matters for the future of the American population.
Source: Duke University

item.description: Clint Black has one of the most storied careers in modern music. He surged to superstardom as part of the fabled Class of ’89, reaching #1 with five consecutive singles from his triple-platinum debut, Killin’ Time. He followed that with the triple-platinum Put Yourself in My Shoes, and then a string of platinum and gold albums throughout the ’90s. Perhaps most impressively, Clint wrote or co-wrote every one of his more than three dozen chart hits, including “A Better Man,” “Killin’ Time,” “When My Ship Comes In,” “A Good Run of Bad Luck,” “Summer’s Comin’,” “Like the Rain,” and “Nothin’ But the Taillights,” part of a catalog that produced 22 #1 singles and made him one of the most successful singer/songwriters of the modern era.
